# Photo Backup — searches to win

Status (2026-11-14): done. Scored Nov 14, 2026 from live web
search of Google Play listings + AppBrain mirrors. Re-score after
launch (ASO skill: monthly refresh) — Play search volume is not
published by Google, so volume is "unknown" for every query below;
demand is read off competitor install velocity instead (see
"Volume: how to read this").

## Volume: how to read this

- Google Play publishes no search-volume numbers, and no free
  public source gives Play keyword volume (checked: Play search
  results via web search, AppBrain app pages). Paid ASO tools
  (Sensor Tower etc.) are the only volume source — not used here.
- Demand proxy used instead: installs of the niche's direct apps.
  Photos to USB: OTG Backup — 270 installs in ~40 days since
  Oct 2026 launch (AppBrain). VaultDrive: USB Photo Backup —
  870 installs total, ~21/day over the last 30 days (AppBrain,
  Nov 14, 2026). The niche has real but small demand; two new
  direct rivals launched Oct 2026 and are both still unrated.
- Re-checked November 21, 2026: AppBrain still reads 870 installs
  for VaultDrive (490 in the last 30 days, ~16/day; last updated
  November 3, 2026), so the November 14 figure above stands;
  VaultDrive's own product page claims 2,000+ installs across the
  App Store and Google Play combined — a different, vendor-claimed
  count, not the Android-only AppBrain figure.
- Difficulty is qualitative, from the size/ratings of the apps
  ranking on top for that query on Nov 14, 2026.

## Scored queries

### 1. "photo backup to usb" — WINNER (tied)
- Volume: unknown (see above). Demand proxy: niche demand, small.
- Difficulty: Medium. The exact-match direct rival on top,
  Photos to USB: OTG Backup, is 270 installs / 0 ratings, but
  the 10M-install Files To SD Card also ranks, so the page is
  not empty.
- Current top apps: 1. Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Akshay C P,
  270 installs, 0 ratings, Oct 2026) · 2. Buffalo Photo Backup
  (~4k installs, 4.5★, Japan) · 3. Files To SD Card, USB or
  Wi-Fi (10M+, 4.5★, ~358k reviews) · 4. PhotoSaver
  Phone-to-Drive (ClevX) · 5. VaultDrive: USB Photo Backup
  (870 installs, 0 ratings, Oct 2026).
- Verdict: keep in title — the current store title already
  contains this phrase verbatim.

### 2. "backup photos to external drive android" — MEDIUM
- Volume: unknown.
- Difficulty: Medium. Broader intent pulls in generic backup
  apps, not just USB-first ones.
- Current top apps: 1. Buffalo Photo Backup · 2. PhotoSaver
  Phone-to-Drive · 3. Backup and Restore All (generic,
  Google Drive/SD/local) · 4. VaultDrive: USB Photo Backup ·
  5. Photos to USB: OTG Backup · 6. Phone Backup Restore OTG
  Tools.
- Verdict: secondary phrase for the full description only;
  too long and too generic for the title.

### 3. "copy photos to usb stick android" — HIGH difficulty
- Volume: unknown.
- Difficulty: High. The 10M-install Files To SD Card tops the
  results, and the query is dominated by how-to web articles
  (Coolmuster, MobiKin, askfilo) — how-to intent, not
  app-discovery intent.
- Current top apps: 1. Files To SD Card, USB or Wi-Fi (10M+,
  4.5★) · 2. Photos to USB: OTG Backup · plus USB OTG Connector
  & Pen Drive (Vizo Apps) and how-to guides, no other
  photo-first backup app.
- Verdict: do not chase. Keep "copy photos to usb stick" as a
  full-description phrase only (it is already close to the
  listing copy).

### 4. "photo backup app offline" — LOW-MEDIUM difficulty, LOW relevance
- Volume: unknown.
- Difficulty: Low-Medium. No USB-first app dominates; the top

- Current top apps: 1. MeBackup — Secure Offline Backup & Sync

### 5. "backup dcim to otg" — VERY LOW difficulty, ~ZERO volume

  note. SnapDisk copies videos (MP4, MOV, MKV, WebM and more)
  the same way it copies photos: oldest-first, byte-for-byte,
  size-verified (PhotoQuery.kt VIDEO_EXTENSIONS).
- Verdict: how-to article material, not a listing keyword.
  Article published Nov 16, 2026 (WL-45, 16th how-to):
  docs/videos-to-usb.html.

  Android, so SnapDisk cannot install on it at all —

  OS too.

  computer or the cloud, never at a USB drive; the Trekker-X4

  backs data up to Google's cloud; a microSD card (up to 512GB

  Case line — no Hard Case model lists USB OTG support in the

  the H570S, the H590S, and the H620S and microUSB 2.0 for the

  H280S, and H242 pages; Google Photos (the stock photo backup on

  the H240S) is a real local copy, but the card stays in the
  phone and needs a reader elsewhere; a computer copy (connect
  the phone to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of

  automatically. Out of scope, named in the article: OTG host
  support is unconfirmed on every Hard Case model, so owners of

  MT6739 / 2 GB / 16 GB / 6500 mAh per phonesdata and specspro);
  the H500S Android version is disputed (8.0 per pkgsm, 7.0 per
  mobilespecs and spec411); the H621S connector is unverified in

  compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day

  of plain photo files on a USB drive.
- What the models mean: four Conquest models cannot run
  SnapDisk at all — the S6 runs Android 5.1, and the S8, the
  S8+, and the S8 Pro run Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android
  7.0 minimum, even though the S8 lists USB OTG support; the
  S9's Android version is disputed (5.1.1 per devicesfaq, 7.1.1
  per trak.in), so check Settings > About phone on that model
  before installing; OTG support is confirmed in the sources
  found only on the S8, which cannot run SnapDisk — on the S10,
  the S12, the S12 Pro, the S16, the S22 5G, and the EX201 it is
  unconfirmed, so owners of those models should plug a drive in
  and check Settings > Storage before relying on it; the USB
  port type is unconfirmed on the S22 5G and the EX201 — the S10
  has micro USB, the S12 and the S16 have USB-C, and the S8 has
  micro USB 2.0 — so owners should check their own port before
  buying an adapter; the S6 comes in two variants (MT6732, 1 GB
  RAM, 8 GB storage, 4000 mAh per Ubergizmo against MT6752,
  3 GB RAM, 32 GB storage, 6000 mAh for the S6 OCTA per
  mobilexfiles), though both run Android 5.1; the S10 takes a
  microSD card up to 128 GB, the S8+ takes one up to 128 GB,
  and the S16 takes one up to 128 GB (ATEX variant up to 2 TB)
  — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later.
- Verdict: how-to article material, not a listing keyword.
  Article published Nov 18, 2026 (WL-88, 57th how-to):
  docs/conquest-photos-to-usb.html.
  Fallback for WL-89: Land Rover Explore — no Land Rover article
  exists in docs/ yet.

  or size verification of every file); PhotoSaver Phone-to-Drive
  (Play listing, com.clevx.photosaver — a second one-tap app
  alternative: save photos and videos to any USB-C drive with
  one click, no cloud, no upload. Generic Android, not a JCB
  guide — but it does work on the current JCB models, since
  all of them have USB-C); cloud routes — Google Photos syncs
  the gallery to Google's servers, Google Drive backs data up
  to Google's cloud with 15 GB free, and Google backup restores
  data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you
  hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses
  photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop
  paying for storage. Neither route gives a folder of plain
  photo files on a USB drive.
  JCB specifics: OTG is confirmed in the sources found on the
  Toughphone, the Toughphone Max, the E10, and the T10 —
  cashify lists "OTG Support, Yes" for the Toughphone and the
  Toughphone Max, the E10 review lists "USB-C 2.0 (OTG)", and
  JCB's own T10 page lists "USB-C with OTG support" — and
  every current model can run SnapDisk: the Toughphone runs
  Android 13, the Toughphone Max runs Android 12, the E10
  runs Android 15, the E50 runs Android 16, and the T10 tablet
  runs Android 16; on the E50 no source found mentions OTG at
  all, so the article tells owners of that model to plug a
  drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it
  instead of claiming OTG across the range. Two old JCB phones
  cannot run SnapDisk at all: the TP802 is a feature phone,
  not an Android phone, and the Toughphone Pro-Smart TP909
  from 2012 runs Android 2.3.5, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0
  minimum. The E10's specs are disputed between sources: one
  review's own spec table says Android 16 while its text and
  JCB's own site say Android 15, its chipset is a Helio G36
  per that review against an MT6765X per Clove and
  rugged.co.uk, and its RAM is 4 GB per that review against
  8 GB per rugged.co.uk — so the chipset and RAM are not leaned
  on in the article, and the Android version is taken as 15
  from JCB's own site. All current models have USB-C. All
  current models take a microSD card — up to 1 TB on the
  Toughphone, the Toughphone Max, and the E50, up to 512 GB on
  the E10, and up to 2 TB on the T10 tablet.
  JCB's own tools: the only JCB file advice found is the old
  TP802 manual's PC copy with a USB cable (Mass Storage); the
  stock photo backup is Google Photos, and the stock file
  manager is Files by Google; a microSD card is the local
  option on every current model; no JCB backup page points at
  a USB drive at all — none of them writes plain photo files
  to a USB drive automatically. Out of scope, named in the
  article: OTG support is unconfirmed on the E50, so owners of
  that model should check Settings > Storage before relying
  on it; the E10's specs are disputed between sources
  (Android 15/16, Helio G36 vs MT6765X, 4 GB vs 8 GB of RAM);
  the TP802 and the Toughphone Pro-Smart TP909 cannot run
  SnapDisk (feature phone / Android 2.3.5) — SnapDisk needs
  Android 7.0 or later.
- Verdict: how-to article material, not a listing keyword.

  guide, the same BlackBerry 10.3 manual and a Porsche Design manual —
  all computer copies or phone-to-phone moves for BlackBerry OS or
  BlackBerry 10 phones, none of them BlackBerry-Android-specific either.
- One-tap proven 6 / mounting test 1 / below floor 3. Ten covered
  BlackBerry Android phones: seven clear Android 7.0 on shipped software,
  the lowest shipped version that clears being Android 7.0 (Aurora).
  USB OTG Yes on six (KEYone, Aurora, KEY2, KEY2 LE, Evolve, Evolve X);
  contested on one (Motion: Gadgets360 and MobileGizmo Yes against
  Notebookcheck's review saying the Type-C port serves solely for charging
  and transferring data, with GSMArena omitting OTG). Three run below
  Android 7.0 (Priv 5.1.1, DTEK50 and DTEK60 6.0.1); the DTEK50 and the
  DTEK60 list USB OTG Yes, so the file-manager copy works on those two,
  while the Priv's OTG is contested (Gadgets360, Notebookcheck and
  malaysianwireless Yes against FoneArena No, GSMArena omitting it).
  Seven take USB Type-C (DTEK60, KEYone, Motion, KEY2, KEY2 LE, Evolve,
  Evolve X) and three take micro-USB (Priv, DTEK50, Aurora). A microSD
  card fits all ten for certain; ceilings are stated on all ten, clean on
  seven (2 TB on DTEK50, DTEK60, KEYone; 256 GB on Aurora, KEY2, KEY2 LE,
  Evolve) and contested on three (Priv: 256 GB against 2 TB; Motion:
  256 GB against 2 TB; Evolve X: 256 GB against 2 TB). The slot is a
  dedicated slot on the Priv and the DTEK60 and a shared SIM slot on the
  DTEK50, the KEYone, the Motion, the KEY2, the KEY2 LE and the Evolve X,
  and the slot type is unstated on two (Aurora, Evolve). VaultDrive needs
  Android 8 or later per its own site, so four clear the version floor and
  all four are proven, while AppBrain lists 12.1 or later, which none
  clears. FotoSafe needs Android 9 or later with USB host or OTG support,
  so none is proven — the highest shipped version is Android 8.1; a 2018
  report listed the KEY2 as eligible for Android 9, but no consulted
  source confirms it shipped. The Motion's Android is three labels — 7.1
  against 7.1.1 against 7.1.2 — but the version is 7.1 either way. The
  DTEK50 and the DTEK60 are rebranded Alcatel phones — the Idol 4 and the
  Idol 4S, per Wikipedia — and TCL made six of the ten phones. The Aurora
  was sold in Indonesia only, by BB Merah Putih, and the Evolve and the
  Evolve X in India only, by Optiemus. TCL stopped making BlackBerry
  phones on August 31, 2020, when the licence ended, and OnwardMobility
  signed a new licence that same month but never released a device before
  shutting down in 2022 — so the KEY2 LE was the last BlackBerry phone
  developed. BlackBerry has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own; the
  Content Transfer app moves data to a new phone over Google Drive or a
  media card, and BlackBerry Link and the Desktop Software copy files to a
  computer. Not covered: BlackBerry Ghost (rumoured, never launched),
  DTEK70 (a rumour), the OnwardMobility 5G phone (never shipped), the
  Zinwa Q25 (a third-party Android conversion of the Classic, not a
  BlackBerry product), and all BlackBerry 10 and BlackBerry OS phones,
  which run BlackBerry 10 or BlackBerry OS, not Android.
- Verdict: how-to article material, not a listing keyword. Article
  drafted Nov 20, 2026 (WL-166, 134th how-to):

### 134. "back up photos from a broken-screen phone to USB drive without computer" — HOW-TO GAP
- Volume: unknown (Play publishes no volume).
- Difficulty: Low. No top result is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB
  backup guide for a broken screen at all, let alone a whole-library
  one-tap backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume — and the two
  real guides in the results describe a manual file copy, not a one-tap

- Current top results (scored Nov 20, 2026, live web search):
  androidauthority.com, "How to recover data from a broken Android phone"
  (https://www.androidauthority.com/extract-data-broken-android-phone-819324/
  — if the data is on an SD card, eject the card and slot it into a
  computer; the safest method is a USB-C to HDMI dongle and an external
  display, with a keyboard and mouse if touch is dead; and it is not
  possible to recover files from a completely dead Android device —
  replace the faulty components or seek help from a data recovery
  professional. A real generic recovery guide, and the source for the
  dead-phone limit — but it offloads files by hand, it is not a one-tap
  whole-library backup, and it says nothing about SnapDisk);
  phoneexpertphonerepair.com, "Recovering Photos from a Broken Phone:
  Proven Steps"
  (https://phoneexpertphonerepair.com/recovering-photos-from-a-broken-phone/
  — check cloud backups first, then a cracked screen with dead touch gets
  an OTG mouse: plug the adapter into the charging port, plug the mouse
  in, a cursor appears, enter your own PIN or pattern — and from there
  copy your photos to a USB drive, upload them to the cloud, or connect
  the phone to a computer; a phone with one port cannot charge while the
  mouse occupies it; a black screen with the phone still on needs a USB-C
  hub with video-out, which only works on supported models and can be
  blocked by an on-screen prompt. A real repair-shop guide that DOES
  mention OTG-mouse unlock and copying photos to a USB drive — but the
  copy it describes is a manual file copy, not a one-tap whole-library
  backup with progress, Pause and Stop, and it says nothing about
  SnapDisk);
  drfone.wondershare.com, "How to Transfer Data from a Phone With a Broken
  Screen: Android & iPhone"
  (https://drfone.wondershare.com/broken-phone-recovery/how-to-transfer-data-from-broken-screen-phone.html
  — sorts broken screens by condition first: a visible screen with dead
  touch gets an OTG mouse to enter your own passcode, with the warning
  that a mouse does not bypass the screen lock; a black screen that still
  powers on needs cloud copies, an external display or repair; a locked or
  black display cannot be treated as an unlocked storage drive. A real
  guide — but its routes run through a computer and its own paid recovery
  software, not a phone-to-USB one-tap backup, and it says nothing about
  SnapDisk);
  drfone.wondershare.com, "How to Get Photos Off a Broken Phone (Android &
  iOS Guide 2026)"
  (https://drfone.wondershare.com/broken-phone-recovery/how-to-get-photos-off-a-broken-phone.html
  — six Android solutions: AutoPlay to a computer, Google Drive, Google
  Photos, its own one-click recovery software, the SD card, and a USB-C
  dongle with an external display. A real guide — but five of the six
  routes need a computer or the cloud, and the sixth is a manual copy
  through a dongle, not a one-tap whole-library backup, and it says
  nothing about SnapDisk).
  Note: a second search surfaced three more of the same shape — Dr.Fone,
  "The Ultimate Guide: Using an Android Phone with a Broken Screen",
  Recoverit, "Android Broken Screen Data Recovery", and Tech Advisor, "How
  to Recover Your Phone Data with a Broken Screen" — an OTG mouse for a
  visible screen with dead touch, a USB-C hub and external display for a
  black screen but only if the model supports DisplayPort Alt Mode or MHL
  video output, ADB only if USB debugging was enabled before the damage,
  Samsung Smart Switch, and the microSD card out through a reader; Recoverit
  warns not to factory reset, flash firmware, or approve any repair that
  wipes the phone before trying the safer options. All real guides — and all
  of them route through a computer, the cloud, or paid recovery software,
  not a phone-to-USB one-tap backup, and none of them mentions SnapDisk.
  SnapDisk's own generic guide
  (https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/usb-photo-backup.html) assumes a
  working screen and says nothing about a mouse, a hub, or a dead phone.
- Three scenarios, three routes. Cracked screen with dead touch and a
  visible display: a USB mouse through an OTG adapter enters your own PIN
  or pattern — a mouse does not bypass the lock — and one tap on SnapDisk's
  notification starts the whole-library backup, oldest-first, with progress,
  Pause and Stop. One port holds either the mouse or the drive, not both,
  so a multi-port OTG hub, or Pro's auto-backup on connect, is what lets
  mouse and drive share the port — and Pro only helps if it was set up
  before the screen broke. Black screen with the phone still powering on:
  a USB-C hub with HDMI and USB ports shows the screen on a monitor, but
  only on phones with DisplayPort Alt Mode video-out — Samsung DeX on the
  Galaxy S8 and later S series, the Note 8 and later, all Z Fold models and
  the A90 5G only; the Z Flip 5 and 6 output video but run no DeX, per XDA,
  and the rest of the A series outputs nothing; Pixel video-out starts at
  the Pixel 8, the Pixel 6 and 7 having USB 3.x ports with display output
  switched off until the Pixel 8; Motorola Edge phones run Ready For, now
  Smart Connect; Huawei Mate and P Pro phones run Easy Projection; Sony
  Xperia 1 and 5, Asus ROG Phones, the LG G8, V50, V60, Velvet and Wing,
  and the Fairphone 5 are listed as supporting video-out too. OnePlus is
  contested — the 12, 13 and Open per the usbctohdmi guide, against the 7
  and newer flagships per the salivity list — so check the exact model
  before buying a hub. Android 16's native desktop mode needs Android 16
  QPR3 or later on a Pixel 8, 9 or 10, per Rayneo; an older Pixel mirrors
  instead. An on-screen prompt can block video-out. A DisplayLink dock is
  a reported workaround for phones without video-out — Faceofit names it as
  the only way an older Pixel 7 can output to a monitor — carried as
  reported, not verified. Completely dead phone: no software route exists —
  Android Authority says so plainly — so check Google Photos and the
  microSD card first, then a screen replacement or professional recovery.
  A microSD card comes out only if the phone takes one — most high-end
  phones no longer do, per Android Authority — and reading the card still
  needs a reader and a computer. SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later
  (minSdk 24 in the repo) and is not on Google Play yet, so install the
  v0.1.2 APK from GitHub. The free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per
  run; Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on
  connect. Drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB —
  SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole
  backup, per the repo README. Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting
  compresses photos, so check that setting before trusting a cloud copy.
  iPhones are not covered — SnapDisk is Android only — and the iPhone OTG
  route varies by model, per the repair-shop guide. FotoSafe needs Android
  9 or later with USB host or OTG support; VaultDrive needs Android 8 or
  later per its own site, Pro $19.99 once, while AppBrain lists 12.1 or
  later. This is the first article in the series about a situation instead
  of a phone brand — the brand series ran to 134 articles.
- Verdict: how-to article material, not a listing keyword. Article

- A low battery is a clock, not a wall — the photos are still on the
  phone, the drive is still in your hand, and the copy is still a
  local one that needs no Wi-Fi and no upload. The copy itself costs
  battery: the drive draws its power from the phone (invotech), and an
  OTG adapter drains the battery quickly (fonelab — charge first if
  you can). The screen is the biggest drain the reader controls: the
  manual copy needs the phone unlocked for the whole transfer
  (mobiletrans), so a manual copy burns battery on the screen, while a
  background copy does not — start it, turn the screen off, and the
  copy runs on its own. The one-port trap is the same class of problem
  as the broken-screen article's: one port holds either the drive or
  the charger, not both, unless the connection goes through a USB-C
  hub with pass-through charging — standard USB-C behaviour, but
  unverified with SnapDisk, so the article says to test it before
  relying on it. The cloud is the worst option on a low battery: it
  needs Wi-Fi, upload time, and free space in the account, and the
  phone burns battery uploading for hours. The repo facts that carry
  the article, read from the code this run: the copy runs as a
  foreground service (dataSync type, BackupService.kt) — the mechanism
  Android gives a copy that must keep running with the screen off —
  but the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling (grep
  over app/src/main, README, and docs finds no WakeLock, PowerManager,
  or power-save code, and the manifest holds no
  REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS), and no low-battery run has
  ever been tested, so screen-off continuation under battery saver is
  unverified and the article says so instead of promising it. What IS
  verified: if the phone dies mid-copy, finished files stay on the
  drive, the file in flight keeps its partial copy, and resume picks up
  where it stopped (byte-exact .part resume, skip-if-exists); and on
  Android 15 and later a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in
  24 hours, so a very long copy can be paused by Android itself, and
  opening the app resets the timer (WL-34). SnapDisk needs Android 7.0
  or later (minSdk 24 in the repo) and is not on Google Play yet, so
  install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub. The free version backs up
  manually up to 5 GB per run, picking up where it stopped past the
  cap — on a low battery that cap is a feature, because a short run
  copies the oldest 5 GB first — which is the case Pro is for; Pro is
  a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect and
  removes the size limit. The screenshot in the article is from
  SnapDisk on a phone — the same settings screen the reader will see.
  The From folder is a picker, not a fixed path — tap it, browse to the
  phone's storage, and choose the folder that holds the photos, which
  the picker reaches because it is the system folder picker, verified
  in the repo as OpenDocumentTree. Drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a
  single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them
  instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README — so use
  exFAT. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes. This is the seventh article
  in the series about a situation instead of a phone brand — the brand
  series ran to 134 articles, and the broken-screen, switching-phones,
  SD-card, tablet, Chromebook, and storage-full articles were the first
  six.

- On the road there is no cloud fallback and no second copy — the
  phone is the only copy until the drive copy finishes and is checked,
  so the backup must COMPLETE and be verified before the phone is
  wiped, lost, or the trip ends. One USB-C port holds the drive OR
  the charger, not both — charge first, or use a powered hub with
  pass-through charging, which is standard USB-C behaviour but
  unverified with SnapDisk; a portable SSD may need a powered hub —
  the phone alone may not supply enough power for both the hub and
  the drive, and shawnmoreton.com says the same. Keep the drive in a
  different bag from the phone — separation is the backup — and copy
  every few days, not on the last night, because a whole trip's
  library is tens of gigabytes and the last night is the worst night
  to start. The cloud copy only counts if it actually uploaded:
  Google Photos backup can be off, it can cover the camera folder
  only, and it can be set to storage saver, which uploads compressed
  copies instead of the originals — seeing a photo in the Photos app
  on the phone proves nothing, because the app shows on-device photos
  too, so the check has to happen at photos.google.com on another
  device — and with no Wi-Fi the upload cannot run at all, so the
  drive copy comes first and the cloud check waits for Wi-Fi. The
  repo facts that carry the article, read from the code this run: the
  copy runs as a foreground service (dataSync type, BackupService.kt)
  — the mechanism Android gives a copy that must keep running with
  the screen off — but the repo holds no wake lock and no
  battery-saver handling (grep over app/src/main finds no WakeLock,
  PowerManager, or power-save code), and no travel run has ever been
  tested, so screen-off continuation under battery saver is
  unverified and the article says so instead of promising it. What IS
  verified: the backup has to finish and be checked before the phone
  is wiped, lost, or the trip ends, and resume covers an interrupted
  copy — finished files stay on the drive, the file in flight keeps
  its partial copy, and resume picks up where it stopped (byte-exact
  .part resume, skip-if-exists, size verification); and on Android 15
  and later a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours, so
  a very long copy can be paused by Android itself, and opening the
  app resets the timer (WL-34). SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later
  (minSdk 24 in the repo) and is not on Google Play yet, so install
  the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub. The free version backs up manually up
  to 5 GB per run, picking up where it stopped past the cap — a trip's
  library is often bigger than 5 GB, so it takes several taps, and
  that is the case Pro is for; Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that
  auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit. The
  screenshot in the article is from SnapDisk on a phone — the same
  settings screen the reader will see. The From folder is a picker,
  not a fixed path — tap it, browse to the phone's storage, and choose
  the folder that holds the photos, which the picker reaches because
  it is the system folder picker, verified in the repo as
  OpenDocumentTree. Drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file
  over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of
  failing the whole backup, per the repo README — so use exFAT.
  SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting photos from the phone
  afterwards is the reader's step, only after verifying photos on the
  drive, and the drive stays in a different bag from the phone. This
  is the tenth article in the series about a situation instead of a
  phone brand — the brand series ran to 134 articles, and the
  broken-screen, switching-phones, SD-card, tablet, Chromebook,
  storage-full, low-battery, factory-reset, and selling-phone articles
  were the first nine.
- Verdict: how-to article material, not a listing keyword. Article
  drafted Nov 20, 2026 (WL-176, 144th how-to):
  docs/traveling-photos-to-usb.html — branch wl-176-traveling.

- Do NOT charge a wet phone and do NOT plug anything into a wet USB
  port — power through a damaged board can burn out the chip that
  holds the photos (mdrepairs: charging "pushes current through a
  corroding board", short circuits "can fry components
  permanently"). The lab's advice conflicts with this article's
  premise and the article states the conflict plainly: the lab says
  power the phone off immediately and do not try to back up your
  photos — this article's route is only for a phone that is on,
  working normally, and has a dry port, and the lab's advice wins
  the moment anything about the phone is wrong. Dry the port first
  (port down, shake the water out); if the phone is off or dead
  there is NO software route — only a recovery lab. Corrosion
  starts within hours and spreads over days (mdrepairs); salt
  water is the worst case. Rice does nothing; a hair dryer pushes
  water deeper. The backup must COMPLETE and be verified on the
  drive before the phone dies — a copy still running when the
  phone dies is not a backup, and there is no undo after. The
  copy runs on the battery the phone has left, because a wet phone
  must not be charged. Cloud-only originals are a trap — Google
  Photos backup can be off, device folders like WhatsApp and
  screenshots may never have been switched on, and storage saver
  uploads are compressed copies, not originals, so check
  photos.google.com before trusting the cloud — and with no Wi-Fi
  the upload cannot run at all, so the drive copy comes first and
  the cloud check waits for Wi-Fi. The repo facts that carry the
  article, read from the code this run: the copy runs as a
  foreground service (dataSync type, BackupService.kt) — the
  mechanism Android gives a copy that must keep running with the
  screen off — but the repo holds no wake lock and no
  battery-saver handling (grep over app/src/main finds no
  WakeLock) and no water-damage run has ever been tested, so
  screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified and
  the article says so instead of promising it. What IS verified:
  oldest-first on MediaStore DATE_TAKEN (BackupEngine.kt,
  PhotoQuery.kt); resume covers an interrupted copy — finished
  files stay on the drive (skip-if-exists with size verification),
  the file in flight keeps its .part copy (byte-exact .part
  resume); on Android 15 and later a dataSync foreground service
  gets 6 hours in 24 hours, so a very long copy can be paused by
  Android itself, and opening the app resets the timer (WL-34);
  the manifest holds no INTERNET permission; SnapDisk copies, it
  never deletes (delete() in BackupEngine.kt touches only .part
  files). SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later (minSdk 24 in the
  repo) and is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK
  from GitHub. The free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per
  run, picking up where it stopped past the cap — a phone that has
  never been backed up often holds a library bigger than 5 GB, so
  it takes several taps, and that is the case Pro is for; Pro is a
  one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect
  and removes the size limit. The screenshot in the article is

  will see. The From folder is a picker, not a fixed path — tap

  holds the photos, which the picker reaches because it is the

  SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing

  brief was NOT verified in the fetched mdrepairs page text (no
  $ amounts in the fetched body) and is NOT used in the article;
  only the $100 diagnostic from the search result text is cited.

  Host/OTG support, and Croma, MySmartPrice, Beebom, and
  Cashify all list OTG as supported, while GSMArena's
  comparison table lists plain USB Type-C with no OTG and
  phonebunch lists OTG as Not Supported — five sources say
  yes, two say no, GSMArena disagreeing with itself, so
  the article tells the reader to plug a drive in and look
  for the mount notification on a CMF Phone 1 before
  buying an adapter. Both phones are USB-C and both clear
  Android 7.0 by a wide margin. Both take a microSD card
  up to 2 TB in a hybrid slot — the one storage option the
  main Nothing phones do not have — named in the article
  as an adjacent route, never as a SnapDisk feature: a card
  in the phone is storage, not a backup, and the slot holds
  the card or a second SIM, not both. Nothing's own tools:
  Google Photos (Photos settings > Backup, to Google's
  cloud, 15 GB free) and Google backup (Settings > Google
  > Backup, Back up by Google One) restore to a new phone
  from the cloud; no Nothing-owned cloud backup for photos
  exists; the gallery app depends on OS version — Google
  Photos on Nothing OS 2.x, Nothing Gallery on Nothing OS
  3.0+ — and Nothing Gallery is a viewer, not a backup
  tool. Stock file manager is Files by Google
  (com.google.android.apps.nbu.files — CMF phones ship
  Google's apps rather than a Nothing-made file manager,
  per the Nothing Community thread in Query 27).
  The repo facts that carry the article, read from the code
  this run: the copy runs as a foreground service
  (dataSync type, BackupService.kt) — the mechanism
  Android gives a copy that must keep running with the
  screen off — but the repo holds no wake lock and no
  battery-saver handling (BackupService.kt has no WakeLock
  and no Doze reference, verified this run) and no CMF run
  has ever been tested, so screen-off continuation under
  battery saver is unverified and the article says so
  instead of promising it. What IS verified: oldest-first
  on MediaStore DATE_TAKEN (BackupEngine.kt,
  PhotoQuery.kt); resume covers an interrupted copy —
  finished files stay on the drive (skip-if-exists with
  size verification), the file in flight keeps its .part
  copy (byte-exact .part resume); on Android 15 and later
  a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours,
  so a very long copy can be paused by Android itself, and
  opening the app resets the timer (WL-34); the manifest
  holds no INTERNET permission; SnapDisk copies, it never
  deletes (delete() in BackupService.kt and BackupEngine.kt
  touches only .part files). SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or
  later (minSdk 24 in the repo) and is not on Google Play
  yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub. The free
  version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run, picking up
  where it stopped past the cap — a phone that has never
  been backed up often holds a library bigger than 5 GB,
  so it takes several taps, and that is the case Pro is
  for; Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts
  the backup on connect and removes the size limit. The
  screenshot in the article is from SnapDisk on a phone —
  the same settings screen the reader will see. The From
  folder is a picker, not a fixed path — tap it, browse to
  the phone's storage, and choose the folder that holds the
  photos, which the picker reaches because it is the system
  folder picker, verified in the repo as OpenDocumentTree
  (MainActivity.kt). Drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a
  single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and
  lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the
  repo README — so use exFAT. Own canonical URL returned
  503 on two checks this run (a control nonexistent slug
  returned 404, so the 503 is specific to this slug, not
  the site) — the article is live only after merge, and
  the 503 is reported, not smoothed over. Title is the
  39-char form "Back up CMF Phone photos to a USB drive"
  — within the ≤53-char brief; the "(no computer)" form
  is carried in the og:title, headline, and breadcrumb.
  This is the 135th article in the brand series — the

### 176. "Back up photos to a VeraCrypt or BitLocker USB drive from Android" — HOW-TO GAP
- Volume: unknown (Play publishes no volume).
- Difficulty: Low on the narrow angle. No guide in search covers a whole-library photo backup
  from an Android phone straight onto a software-encrypted USB drive — VeraCrypt, LUKS, or
  BitLocker — one tap, background with progress, Pause and Stop, resume and verification,
  writing plain files onto the mounted volume. The mounting apps copy by hand, the container
  browsers open a few files, the BitLocker reader copies to internal storage, and the
  encrypted-stick results are product pitches. The gap stands ONLY on that narrow angle: the
  software-encrypted volume mounted on the phone, with the mount, the manual copy, and the
  honest statement about SnapDisk in one guide. The hardware-encrypted-drive half of this
  topic is already covered by our own WL-212 article (Query 172) and is NOT repeated here.
- Current top results (scored Nov 23, 2026, live web search):
  Phrasing 1, "back up photos to encrypted USB drive from Android phone OTG" (supervisor,
  verified this run, not re-run): our own Huawei article (Huawei Backup encrypted archive,
  Huawei-only restore), Dr.Fone generic OTG manual copy, a LESOGE encrypted-stick product
  page, an alibaba generic whole-phone backup guide, and the OTG Master F-Droid page (a tool
  page, not a photo-backup guide). No dedicated guide for whole-library photo backup to an
  encrypted USB drive.
  Phrasing 2, "transfer photos to VeraCrypt BitLocker encrypted USB drive Android phone"
  (supervisor, verified this run, not re-run): OTG Master (interfaces.one +
  moylali.github.io), rottenwifi EDS NG VeraCrypt-open guide (browse/copy a few files;
  filesystem mount needs root), androidcrypt F-Droid page (container browsing), NTFS Reader
  Softonic page (BitLocker decrypt + copy-to-internal; NTFS read-only). Again, no
  whole-library photo-backup guide.
  Phrasing 3 (lead, this run), "backup photos to BitLocker USB drive from Android without
  computer": the top four results are all our own articles — Samsung, automatic transfer,
  Pixel, Xiaomi — generic USB backup guides that never mention BitLocker at all. No dedicated
  guide in any phrasing; the gap stands on the software-encrypted-volume angle.
- Honest centre (verified from the code at base 048414c and live pages this run, Nov 23,
  2026, not assumed): Android reads no VeraCrypt / LUKS / BitLocker volume natively. OTG
  Master (app.fayaz.otgmaster, free, open source GPL-3.0, F-Droid + Google Play, v0.5.2,
  updated Nov 17, 2026, Android 8.0+, no root) mounts VeraCrypt, LUKS1, LUKS2, and BitLocker
  (password, 48-digit recovery key, .BEK key file from 0.5.4) and exposes the unlocked volume
  via DocumentsProvider so Files and other apps can browse it; filesystems inside: FAT32,
  exFAT, NTFS, ext4. No kernel mount on non-rooted Android — userspace USB mass storage
  (libaums), verified from the project's own docs page this run. VeraCrypt limits: SHA-256,
  Whirlpool, Streebog header KDFs not supported; LUKS2 other ciphers refused. SnapDisk
  itself cannot unlock an encrypted drive: 0 matches for encrypt/cipher/AES/decrypt in
  app/src/main, and the copy is a byte copy with a size check only
  (BackupEngine.copyWithResume, BackupEngine.kt:130; verify, BackupEngine.kt:107; Copied
  only after verify passes, BackupEngine.kt:126). Whether SnapDisk's To folder picker can
  write to an OTG Master-mounted volume is UNVERIFIED: no real-device test has been run. The
  code maps the picked SAF tree URI back to a raw /storage/<volume>/<path> path
  (BackupService.destinationBaseDir, BackupService.kt:592-608) and writes plain files there,
  so a DocumentsProvider volume with no such path is expected not to work — but that is a
  reading of the code, not a test; what would prove it is picking a mounted VeraCrypt volume
  as the To folder on a real phone and running a backup. NTFS-inside-encrypted: NTFS Reader
  (Softonic, updated Nov 20, 2026) decrypts BitLocker To Go and copies to internal storage;
  NTFS is read-only on the free tier, NTFS write is a one-time in-app purchase, exFAT/FAT32
  inside BitLocker read+write free. EDS NG (Sovworks, AppBrain 2.55 from 326 ratings, 46
  thousand installs, updated Sep 10, 2026, no ads): browse inside the app, filesystem mount
  needs root. androidcrypt (F-Droid, MIT, free, Android 7.0+, v1.0.16, Aug 17, 2026): browse
  + copy files between device and VeraCrypt containers, FAT32 only. LESOGE 128 GB encrypted
  drive (retailer page + manual, read this run): Touch ID/passcode encryption, one-click
  backup via its dedicated app — but on Android no app is required and the manual says to
  copy by hand in the file manager; the one-click backup and encryption belong to the iOS
  app. Huawei Backup encrypted archive: archive only a Huawei phone restores (our own Huawei
  article). SnapDisk facts from the code at base: Pro $9.99 once (ProPrefs.kt:40, pro_unlock),
  5 GB free per-run cap (ProPrefs.kt:43), oldest-first MediaStore DATE_TAKEN
  (PhotoQuery.kt:23-35, :47, :56-58), size verification after copy (BackupEngine.kt:107,
  :126), Pause/Stop in the notification (BackupService.kt:113-115), foreground-service
  dataSync (AndroidManifest.xml:38), FAT32 >=4 GiB skip (BackupService.kt:428-433), no
  restore function, no WakeLock/Doze code — screen-off continuation under battery saver is
  unverified. "SnapDisk copies, it never deletes" present.
- Anti-duplicate check (first, before writing — the WL-189 lesson): the brief's suggested

  live this run, Nov 23, 2026, not assumed): work and personal profiles have separate
  storage areas — Android Developers, Work profiles: "Since the personal and work profiles
  have separate storage areas, a file URI that is valid on one profile is not valid on the
  other." By default most intents do not cross from one profile to the other, and the
  profile admin decides which intents are allowed to cross — "there's no way for you to
  know in advance which intents are allowed to cross this boundary." Sharing work to
  personal is blocked by default on personally-owned devices (Bayton, cross-profile data
  sharing: copy work to personal blocked by default, personal to work permitted); Intune
  "Device default" blocks sharing from the personally-owned work profile to the personal
  profile, and the admin must set "No restrictions on sharing" to open it. Managed Play:
  an admin can block apps from unknown sources with DISALLOW_INSTALL_UNKNOWN_SOURCES
  (Android Developers, DPC security) — SnapDisk is not on Google Play at all, so it
  cannot be installed from the managed Play Store, and side-loading inside the work
  profile is usually IT-blocked; do NOT claim the work-profile install route works.
  Whether a USB drive appears in the work profile's Files app is UNVERIFIED from
  documentation — no source found this run answers it either way; the article says to
  try it and fall back if the drive doesn't show up. Profile removal deletes local data:
  Android Enterprise Help, quoted by umatechnology: "After the Work Profile is deleted,
  all local data on the device within that profile is deleted." Removal route (Pixel):
  Settings > Passwords, Passkeys & Accounts > Remove work profile > Delete; Samsung steps
  vary. Standard Android device backup may be unavailable on a managed phone. SnapDisk
  facts from the code at base: Pro $9.99 once (ProPrefs.kt:40, pro_unlock :37), 5 GB free
  per-run cap (ProPrefs.kt:43), oldest-first MediaStore DATE_TAKEN (PhotoQuery.kt:23-35,

- Difficulty: Low on the narrow angle. No guide in search covers the joined job —
  a Viber photo, out of the chat and into the gallery via "Save to gallery",
  onto a USB drive plugged into the phone, no computer — with the Viber Images
  folder stated (sdcard/Viber/media/Viber Images), the setting's non-retroactivity
  stated, and the hidden-cache direct-pick question marked honestly. Our own
  generic USB articles rank top and never mention Viber; the Viber guides stop
  at the gallery or at Google Drive cloud backup; the OTG guides never mention
  Viber. The gap stands ONLY on that narrow angle: the Viber photo, out of the
  chat, onto a USB drive, no computer, with the default run proven to cover
  gallery-saved Viber photos and the cache pick marked unverified.
- Current top results (scored Nov 24, 2026, live web search):
  Phrasing 1, "back up Viber photos to USB drive Android no computer"
  (lead, this run): our own usb-photo-backup.html and
  transfer-photos-to-usb-automatically.html rank top and contain 0 "Viber"
  mentions (verified by grep); the rest are Viber's Google Drive cloud backup
  (tehnoblog guide, Facebook walkthrough) and a PC phone-transfer tool
  (MobileTrans, moves Viber chats between phones through a computer). No
  dedicated Viber-photos-to-USB how-to.
  Phrasing 2, "transfer Viber photos to USB stick OTG Android"
  (lead, this run): generic OTG copy guides only (YouTube, Wondershare,
  Coolmuster, EyeFi forum) — plug the drive in, select the photos in the
  file manager, copy them to the drive — none mentions Viber, the "Save to
  gallery" setting, or the Viber Images folder. No dedicated guide.
  Phrasing 3, "Viber save photos to gallery Android folder location Viber
  Images" (lead, fact check, this run): bestim, itoolab, Coolmuster, ik4
  agree — "Save to gallery" under More, Settings, Media (older: Media and
  Storage); received photos save to the gallery in the "Viber Images" album
  at sdcard/Viber/media/Viber Images; manual save is tap the photo, Share,
  "Save to Gallery"; with the setting off, photos sit temporarily in a
  hidden cache folder reported as .viber or .viber media; videos go to
  Viber Videos. No dedicated Viber-photos-to-USB how-to.
- Honest centre (verified from the code at base ead10c4 and the live sources
  above, this run, Nov 24, 2026, not assumed): a photo someone sends you on
  Viber is not in your gallery until you put it there. Turn on "Save to
  gallery" (More, Settings, Media; older: Media and Storage) and every photo
  you receive is saved to the gallery automatically, in the "Viber Images"
  album at sdcard/Viber/media/Viber Images; videos go to a sibling Viber
  Videos folder. The setting is NOT retroactive — photos received before you
  turned it on stay in the chat until you save them one by one (tap the
  photo, Share, "Save to Gallery"). SnapDisk's default run covers the saved
  photos with no folder to pick — proven, not assumed: it reads MediaStore
  images + videos with no folder filter (PhotoQuery.kt:28-44), and a
  Viber-saved photo shows in the gallery as the "Viber Images" album, and
  gallery apps read the media index, so a photo the gallery shows is a photo
  the default run sees. The album's existence in the gallery is the evidence
  the folder is indexed: if Viber placed a .nomedia file in Viber Images,
  the media scanner would skip it and the album would not appear in the
  gallery at all; it does appear, in every guide, so there is no such file.
  When "Save to gallery" is off, received photos sit only in Viber's
  temporary cache, in a hidden folder reported as .viber or .viber media —
  the exact path is UNVERIFIED, the guides disagree on the name — and the
  default run cannot see it at all, because a dot-prefixed folder never
  enters the media index. UNVERIFIED, marked as such in the article: whether
  SnapDisk's From folder picker can open that hidden cache folder directly —
  the picker is the system folder picker (MainActivity.kt:62, OpenDocumentTree)
  opening with no folder pre-selected, no initial-folder hint anywhere in the
  code, no Viber path handling anywhere in the app (0 matches for
  Viber/.viber in the source), and the system picker hides dot-folders — and
  whether the cached photo survives long enough to copy. The honest Method 1
  is the joined workflow: turn on "Save to gallery" first (restart Viber
  after turning it on — one guide says the setting needs the restart), check
  the "Viber Images" album appeared, then run SnapDisk's default backup or
  point the From picker at the Viber folder. Contrast honestly with Viber's
  own Google Drive backup (a restore point for Viber, not plain photo files
  on a drive — the files sit in Viber's backup, not as pictures you can open
  from a USB stick) and PC phone-transfer tools (move chats between phones
  through a computer — a different job). SnapDisk facts re-verified from the
  code at base ead10c4: Pro $9.99 once (ProPrefs.kt:40, PRO_PRICE_LABEL
  "$9.99"), 5 GB free per-run cap (ProPrefs.kt:43, 5L * 1024 * 1024 * 1024),
  oldest-first MediaStore DATE_TAKEN (PhotoQuery.kt:47, :56-59, sort
  DATE_TAKEN ASC with DATE_MODIFIED fallback), size verification after copy
  (BackupEngine.kt:107,108), Pause/Stop in the notification
  (NotificationHelper.kt:126,128,136,138; BackupService.kt:113,115), FAT32
  files >=4 GiB skipped with their reason (BackupService.kt:428-433),
  default From /sdcard/DCIM and To /disk/DCIM (BackupPrefs.kt:50,53), no
  INTERNET permission (0 occurrences in the manifest), no Google Play
  Services dependency (0 matches for com.google.android.gms / play-services
  in the build; only Play Billing, billing-ktx 7.1.1, libs.versions.toml:50),
  no all-files access (no MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE anywhere), minSdk 24
  (Android 7.0). "SnapDisk copies, it never deletes" present — the only
  .delete() calls in the code are on SnapDisk's own half-finished .part files
  (BackupEngine.kt:176, :207; BackupService.kt:385, :477). The article carries
  no install count for SnapDisk (none exists) and no VaultDrive install
  figure.
